title: Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star
notes: Right hand in C position (the A is a small stretch of the 5th finger); left hand plays whole-note and half-note C-position chords.

title: Mary Had a Little Lamb
notes: Right hand stays in C position (C-G); left hand holds C and G notes.

title: Frère Jacques
notes: Melody in the right hand around C position (the A4 in bars 5-6 and the low G3 of the closing ding-dang-dong need small extensions); left hand alternates C and G.

title: Hot Cross Buns
notes: The mi-re-do tune that method books teach first, in C position for both hands. Four bars.

title: Alle meine Entchen (All My Little Ducklings)
notes: The German counting-up children's song, five bars as the reference notates it. Right hand C4 to A4; left hand plays I, IV and V roots in half and whole notes.

title: Lightly Row (Hänschen klein)
notes: The German folk tune 'Hänschen klein', known in English method books as 'Lightly Row', in C. The repeat of the first strain is written out with both endings.

title: Au clair de la lune
notes: First verse in quarter and half notes. The right hand stays in one position, A3 to E4, and reaches down to G3 at the end of the middle phrase ('Ma chandelle est morte'); the left hand sits below it.

title: London Bridge Is Falling Down
notes: The first verse in C, 2/4, with its dotted opening figure; the left hand holds C and G.

title: Old MacDonald Had a Farm
notes: One verse in G major. The 'here a moo, there a moo' bars repeat one note in the right hand over open fifths in the left.

title: Kuckuck, Kuckuck, ruft's aus dem Wald (Cuckoo)
notes: The cuckoo-call spring song in G major, 3/4: the upper voice of the reference's two-part setting, over single bass notes.

title: Little Jack Horner
notes: The nursery-rhyme tune as Walter Crane's The Baby's Opera printed it in 1877, a semitone higher (F instead of E major), 6/8, eight bars. Alfred Moffat printed the same tune in F in 1911. The tune now commonly associated with the rhyme, first printed by J. W. Elliott in 1870, is a different one.

title: See-Saw, Margery Daw
notes: The see-saw rhyme as Lucy Crane set it in The Baby's Bouquet (1878), F major, 6/8, eight bars. This is Crane's tune, not the one commonly sung, which J. W. Elliott first printed in 1870.

title: Schlaf, Kindlein, schlaf (Sleep, Baby, Sleep)
composer: Johann Friedrich Reichardt (after a folk tune)
notes: The German lullaby in Johann Friedrich Reichardt's melody of 1781, as the German Wikipedia article prints it, in C instead of F, 2/4, ten bars. The English article's version differs in bars 2 to 4.

title: Little Bo-Peep
notes: The nursery-rhyme tune as Alfred Moffat printed it in Our Old Nursery Rhymes (1911), F major, 6/8, eight bars, one verse. The right hand stays in F position throughout; bar 4's thirds in the source are played as their top notes.

title: The Three Little Kittens
notes: The tune Lucy Crane collected and arranged for The Baby's Bouquet (1878), a fourth lower (F instead of B-flat major), 6/8 with a sixteenth-note pickup, eight bars, one verse with its 'Mew, mew' refrain. The right hand stays in C position with the A as its one extension.

title: Jingle Bells (chorus)
notes: Chorus only. Right hand in C position; left hand plays C, F and G7 harmonies as held notes.

title: Jolly Old Saint Nicholas
notes: Arranged in G major (the 1881 source is in A major). Right hand single notes from D4 to B4; left hand half notes on G, A, B, C and D with open fifths at the start, the middle and the end. The words are Emily Huntington Miller's 1865 poem; the music is generally attributed to James R. Murray (School Chimes, 1874).

title: When the Saints Go Marching In
notes: The traditional tune, not the similarly titled 1896 hymn 'When the Saints Are Marching In' (Katharine Purvis and James M. Black). Written in 4/4 with the reference's 2/4 values doubled, so the beginner reads quarter and half notes. Left hand on C and G, with F under the IV chord.

title: Michael, Row the Boat Ashore
year: printed 1867 (Slave Songs of the United States)
notes: The spiritual first printed in Slave Songs of the United States (1867), in the familiar version of the Wikipedia score, one verse. Right hand C4 to A4; left hand plays I, IV and V roots in whole and half notes.

title: Camptown Races
notes: Original title 'Gwine to Run All Night' (F. D. Benteen, Baltimore, 1850). The verse only, arranged in C major (the source is in D major) with the note values doubled; the chorus climbs to the upper octave and is left out.

title: Oh! Susanna
notes: Verse 1 and the chorus, played once, in the source's key of G major with the note values doubled; the dotted eighth-sixteenth pairs are straightened.

title: Long, Long Ago
notes: Written in 1833; the earliest edition found is Cramer, Addison & Beale's (London), advertised in February 1839, a few weeks before Bayly's death. The first eight bars only (the A section, ending on the tonic), in the source's key of F major; the middle section drops to C4 and is left out.

title: Little Brown Jug
notes: Published under the pen name 'Eastburn'. The chorus only ('Ha, ha, ha, you and me'), in the source's key of C major with the note values doubled; the verse reaches down to E4 and is left out.

title: Ode to Joy (simplified)
notes: Theme simplified to stay in C position for the right hand; left hand plays open fifths and single notes.

title: Pease Porridge Hot
notes: The clapping game as printed in The Song Play Book (1922), G major: the claps on beat 4 are rests.

title: Scarborough Fair
notes: Traditional Dorian melody with an open-fifth accompaniment; deliberately avoids the copyrighted 1966 Simon & Garfunkel arrangement and its 'Canticle' counter-melody.

title: Greensleeves
notes: Melody in A minor (6/8) over dotted-half bass notes and simple chords.

title: Yankee Doodle
year: 18th century (the tune appears in the ballad opera The Disappointment, 1762)
notes: Verse and chorus as in the reference, transposed from A to G major with the note values doubled; the chorus is louder. Left hand: G and D half notes under the verse, C, G and D major triads under the chorus.

title: Auld Lang Syne
year: tune first printed 1799 (George Thomson, Select Songs of Scotland); words Robert Burns, 1788
notes: The whole tune in F major over open fifths (F, C, B-flat and G minor), one per bar or half bar.

title: Sakura, Sakura
year: first printed 1888 (Sokyokushu, Japanese Ministry of Education)
notes: The whole song as first printed in 1888, without key signature (A minor), over open fifths; it ends on an open fifth on E, the tune's final.

title: Korobeiniki (The Peddlers)
composer: Traditional (Russian), in the setting attributed to Yakov Prigozhy
notes: The folk song (not the 1989 video-game arrangement), with the repeat of the second strain written out, over A minor, D minor and E major triads. The music was first printed in 1898; the Russian Wikipedia names Yakov Prigozhy's setting as the most popular version.

title: La Cucaracha
year: 19th century (verses documented from 1819; popular in the 1910s)
notes: Chorus, verse and chorus again in F major (3/4), over open fifths on F, C and G.

title: Red River Valley
year: first sheet music 1896 (as 'In the Bright Mohawk Valley', credited to James J. Kerrigan); words printed 1887
notes: Spare used in place of Shenandoah (no notated source). The tune twice, as verse and refrain, in G major: open fifths in the first stanza, broken fifths in the second. The first sheet music (New York, 1896) names James J. Kerrigan as writer, but the song circulated before: a lyric manuscript annotated 'Nemaha 1879' and 'Harlan 1885', and a readers' request for the words in The Weekly Wisconsin in June 1887, printed there that September; the English Wikipedia gives the writer as 'Traditional'.

title: Loch Lomond
year: earliest known sheet music 1840 or 1841 (Paterson and Sons, Edinburgh)
notes: Spare used in place of the Londonderry Air (its melody is too wide for level 2). Verse and chorus in F major as edited by Robert Ford: held triads under the verse, root and fifth under the chorus. The Scotch snaps and dotted pairs are played as even eighths. Lady John Scott (1810-1900), sometimes credited, only noted down the song she heard sung, per the English Wikipedia; the composer is unknown.

title: Silent Night (Stille Nacht)
notes: The contemporary melody in C major over open fifths on C, G and F, with a fifth on D under 'sleep in heavenly peace'.

title: Joy to the World
notes: Lowell Mason's tune Antioch in D major; the left hand stays around D3 to A3 with open fifths on D.

title: O Come, All Ye Faithful (Adeste Fideles)
notes: The hymn tune in G major; the left hand plays open fifths and single notes, changing harmony at most twice a bar.

title: Deck the Halls
notes: The 1881 version (without the middle fa-la-la of later versions), with its repeated second half written out. Left hand open fifths on F, C, G and B-flat.

title: Good King Wenceslas
notes: Arranged in G major (the source is in A major) in 4/4; the left hand plays open fifths on G, C, D, A and E.

title: O Christmas Tree (O Tannenbaum)
notes: Anschütz's 1824 tune with its middle section and the da capo written out; open fifths on G, A, C and D in the left hand.

title: The First Noel
notes: Verse 1 and the chorus as printed by Bramley and Stainer, over open fifths on D, G, A and B.

title: Amazing Grace
notes: Melody in F major over a simple bass with held chords.

title: Old Hundredth
notes: The psalm tune of the Genevan Psalter in its original rhythm (long first and last notes in each line), sung in English to 'All people that on earth do dwell' and the Doxology. Barred in 4/4; the left hand gives one triad per half bar.

title: Holy, Holy, Holy (tune Nicaea)
notes: Dykes's tune for Reginald Heber's hymn, after the New English Hymnal setting, with the 4/2 values halved into 4/4. The left hand simplifies the hymnal's lower three voices to one triad per half bar.

title: A Mighty Fortress Is Our God (Ein feste Burg)
catalogue: chorale melody, as set by J. S. Bach in BWV 80
notes: Spare for this task, replacing Swing Low, Sweet Chariot (no reliable notated source). Luther's chorale in the even rhythm of Bach's closing chorale of the cantata BWV 80, with the repeat of the first two lines written out and the fermatas left out.

title: La Marseillaise
catalogue: Chant de guerre pour l'Armée du Rhin
notes: The melody of the first edition (Bignon, 1792) as typeset for Mutopia, with the sixteenth-note pickups straightened to eighths and the closing ritornello left out. Left hand: half-bar triads and single bass notes.

title: God Save the King
notes: The British national anthem (the same tune as 'My Country, 'Tis of Thee'), in F major. Left hand one triad per bar, two or three in the cadences.

title: Austrian Hymn (Gott erhalte Franz den Kaiser)
notes: Spare for this task, replacing Simple Gifts (no readable notated source). Haydn's hymn for Emperor Francis II, first performed on 12 February 1797; the tune of the hymn 'Austria' and of 'Das Lied der Deutschen'. Both repeats written out.

title: Happy Birthday to You
composer: Mildred J. Hill and Patty Hill
notes: In the public domain in the United States since the 2016 settlement of Marya v. Warner/Chappell (the court found no valid copyright in the lyrics, 2015); in the EU the song entered the public domain on 1 January 2017. Melody spans an octave, so it needs one hand shift.

title: Daisy Bell (A Bicycle Built for Two)
notes: Harry Dacre was the pen name of Frank Dean. The chorus only ('Daisy, Daisy, give me your answer do'), in the source's key of G major, with a waltz bass.

title: In the Good Old Summer Time
notes: A spare of the L1 plan, used in place of maple-leaf-rag-easy (see 'rejected'). Words by Ren Shields (1868-1913), which are not printed. The chorus only, once with its second ending, in the source's key of B-flat major, with a waltz bass.

title: The Entertainer, A strain (simplified)
notes: The first strain (A strain) of The Entertainer as a single melody line over a simplified stride bass, in the original key of C major with the note values doubled. The library also has the complete rag (joplin-the-entertainer).

title: Canon in D (simplified)
notes: Easy arrangement in augmentation (half notes, as in most easy editions): the left hand plays the famous eight-note ground bass, the right hand the first two lines of the first violin, which move in 3rds and 5ths against the bass.

title: Theme from the "Surprise" Symphony
notes: The first violins' theme (bars 1-16), played softly the second time and ending with the famous fortissimo chord, here in the left hand. First published in 1795 (Offenbach: André, according to IMSLP).

title: Lullaby (Wiegenlied)
notes: Arranged in F major (the song is in E-flat major). First published by Simrock in November 1868 (IMSLP).

title: Eine kleine Nachtmusik, opening theme
catalogue: Serenade in G major, K. 525, 1st movement (opening)
notes: The four opening bars of the first movement, an octave lower than the violins. First published about 1827 (Offenbach: André, according to IMSLP).

notes: From the 1725 Notebook for Anna Magdalena Bach; long attributed to J. S. Bach, now to Christian Petzold. Engraved from the Bach-Gesellschaft edition.

title: Minuet in B-flat major
notes: Mutopia edition contributor: Steven McDougall. Source edition and licence in fetched RDF. Fresh online recheck 2026-10-15; Both MIDI comparisons are exact; MusicXML schema validation and medium/large playability gates pass. Anonymous notebook composition, traditionally attributed to Bach; BWV Anh. 118. Engraved from Bach-Gesellschaft volume 43 (1894), Public Domain dedication by Steven McDougall (Mutopia 1014). Two syntax-only catalog patches normalize the source's terminal rehearsal-mark fermata glyphs to directed note fermatas on the same final second-ending dotted halves (upright above the right hand, inverted below the left); the original markup marks are removed. Pitches, onsets, durations and MIDI remain unchanged.

title: Minuet in A minor
notes: From the 1725 Notebook for Anna Magdalena Bach; anonymous (Mutopia files it under J. S. Bach). Engraved from the Bach-Gesellschaft edition, vol. 43 (1894). The source has no key signature command; keyName gives the key. Two catalog patches: the source pads the half-bars 12 and 28 with an invisible spacer rest in each staff and starts the second half with \partial 4, which makes LilyPond 2.24 insert an extra beat after bar 12 and makes the converter drop the final repeat sign; the four spacers are removed, so that the upbeat completes bar 12 and the last bar complements it, as in the Bach-Gesellschaft edition, and the upbeat G gets its quarter-note duration written out (it inherited the spacer's). The LilyPond 2.24 MIDI check is exact (165/165). Accepted difference in the published-MIDI check only: the Mutopia MIDI (LilyPond 2.12) keeps the spacer beat, so every note from the second half's upbeat on sounds one quarter later; shifted by that quarter it equals the score note for note (90 notes, checked 2026-10-14).

title: Little Prelude in C major (Clavier-Büchlein for W. F. Bach)
notes: From the Clavier-Büchlein vor Wilhelm Friedemann Bach (begun 1720). Mutopia title '9 Little Preludes - 1 - C Major'. Engraved by JD Erickson from the Bach-Gesellschaft edition (1853). Ernst Naumann, 1890). The engraving is CC BY-SA 3.0 (attribution: Hajo Dezelski / Mutopia Project); this MusicXML is shared under the same license.

title: Applicatio in C major
notes: The first piece of the Clavier-Büchlein vor Wilhelm Friedemann Bach (1720), a fingering lesson: Bach's manuscript carries his own fingerings. This engraving reproduces the Bach-Gesellschaft text without them, so there is no editorial-fingering copy. Engraved by Allen Garvin and placed in the public domain. Both halves repeat (written once, with repeat signs).

title: Rondo in C major
excerpt: Bars 1-24 of 56: the C major theme up to the Fine, ending on the tonic; the F major middle section (bars 25-56) and its 'D.C. al Fine' are left out, because the score cannot play the da capo back.
notes: Johann Baptist Wanhal (Jan Křtitel Vaňhal). Engraved from an unnamed late 19th-century edition. The piece is in three parts: a C major theme (bars 1-24, marked 'Fine'), an F major middle section (bars 25-56) and 'D.C. al Fine'. The converter writes the 'D.C. al Fine' as text only (no <sound dacapo/fine>, and the app has no da capo playback), and Mutopia's own MIDI also stops at bar 56, so the whole score would play back ending in F major, with a listed duration (about 62 s) that leaves out the da capo (about 89 s with it). The excerpt keeps the theme, a musical whole of 24 bars that ends on the tonic; barTo 24 makes both MIDI checks compare bars 1-24. Writing the da capo out with a patch would diverge from the engraving.

title: Minuet in C major
excerpt: Bars 1-16 of 32: the C major minuet theme through the Fine; the F major contrasting section and D.C. al Fine are omitted.
notes: Mutopia edition contributor: Bas Wassink. Source edition and licence in fetched RDF. Fresh online recheck 2026-10-15; Both MIDI comparisons are exact; MusicXML schema validation and medium/large playability gates pass. Engraved from an unnamed late-19th-century edition (Mutopia 191, Public Domain). The source header prints Menuett although its Mutopia metadata calls it Rondo. The full source ends with D.C. al Fine, which the converter stores as text and the app cannot execute; this excerpt keeps the complete 16-bar C major theme ending on tonic, rather than ending playback in F major. No notes altered.

title: Polska from Norrbotten
catalogue: Traditioner af Swenska Folk-Dansar, part 1, No. 1
collection: Swedish folk dances (Traditioner af Swenska Folk-Dansar, 1814)
notes: Mutopia title 'Traditioner af Swenska Folk-Dansar, 1st part, nr 1' (a polska from Norrbotten, Sweden), engraved from the 1814 collection. The engraving is CC BY 2.5 (attribution: Erik Sjölund / Mutopia Project, piece 815); this MusicXML is shared under the same licence with the same attribution. Two catalog patches: the three bars of measured tremolo in the left hand (\repeat tremolo 6 <d d'>8) are written out as the six eighth-note octaves they abbreviate, which is what both MIDI files play; and the source's separate MIDI \score no longer unfolds the repeat, so the LilyPond 2.24 check compares the notes as written (exact, 211/211; xmlcheck counts grace notes once, so an unfolded comparison would report the second pass's grace notes). Accepted difference in the published-MIDI check only: matched 422/422 with the repeat unfolded; its two extra notes are the D5 grace notes of the second pass, for the same reason. Bar 1 shows an mf that the source hides (\once \override DynamicText #'transparent = ##t in its dynamics variable), so Mutopia's PDF prints no dynamic there; the converter does not carry the transparency over. Playback is unaffected.
